newsitem.title: USA: Roth bill has something for everyone in munis.
newsitem.headline: Roth bill has something for everyone in munis.

text.p: The tax plan announced by U.S. Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth on Tuesday has a little something in it for all segments of the tax-exempt bond market, municipal bond lobbyists said.

For instance, said Amy Dunbar, director of governmental affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, Roth's proposed repeal of the current $150 million limit on 501(c)(3) bond volume is good news for not-for profits organizations like universities, nursing homes and museums.
By contrast, the House Ways and Means Committee last week approved a narrower expansion of the 501(c)(3) volume cap from $150 million to only $200 million over five years.

Michael Decker, vice president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, noted that Roth's language is similar to a proposal by Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, D-N.Y. calling for repeal of the 501(c)(3) bond cap.
But Roth's bill does not include a controversial Moynihan proposal to bar the use of tax exempt bonds for professional sports stadiums, Decker noted, adding to the good news for the muni market.
Dunbar said that governmental issuers will be pleased that Roth's bill would not roll back the two percent de minimis rule for corporate holdings of municipal bonds.

Meanwhile, Ways and Means voted to scale back the de minimis exemption for corporate holdings of munis to a flat $1 million, which lobbyists said would virtually gut the provision for the muni market.

Governmental issuers also "got a little help on school construction," Dunbar said. She was referring to Roth's proposal to raise the small issuer arbitrage rebate exception for governmental bonds used to finance education facilities from $5 million to $10 million.
The Ways and Means bill includes some minor so-called bond simplification provisions but not the $10 million small issuer rebate exception.
The Government Finance Officers Assocation last week sent an "Urgent Legislative Alert" asking localities to lobby Roth to include that and one other key provision in his bill.
GFOA also wants a safe harbor from arbitrage rules for issuers that reasonably expect to spend 15 percent of bond proceeds within 12 months and 95 percent within three years of issuance.
Neither Roth's bill nor that cleared by Ways and Means includes the provision.

Dunbar said industrial development bond issuers will be pleased with Roth's proposal to increase the size of projects that can be financed with small-issue tax-exempt bonds, from $10 million to $20 million, although the bond cap would remain at $10 million.
"Overall, it's not a bad bill at all," Decker said.

But, in a disappointment to muni market participants, neither the House or Senate bills seeks repeal of the corporate alternative minimum tax, which would have beefed up demand for long-term munis by property and casualty companies.
